comment: What must not silently disappear from issueflow. `prose` names guardrails no code enforces; `split` declares which half of the skill is deterministic; `baseline` names the offline, $0 checks pinned against a real run.

prose.pattern: No stage runs on anything but its predecessor's artifact, ap
prose.rationale: The one rule. It is the reason this skill exists rather than a prompt; lose the line and the skill becomes a generic assistant with extra steps.

prose.pattern: Never claim a result you did not observe
prose.rationale: Honesty about what was verified is the whole house contract. A skill that reports success it did not witness is worse than one that reports nothing.

prose.pattern: never ask about anything in it
prose.rationale: Two questions maximum is only achievable because detection already answered the rest. Asking about a detectable signal is the UX failure that makes a skill feel like a form.

prose.pattern: Never dispatch a stage on a model other than the one
prose.rationale: The per-stage model is the whole reason this is four subagents rather than one loop: investigation and design get the strongest model because a wrong answer there is cheapest to produce and most expensive to find. An orchestrator that quietly runs everything on one model has kept the ceremony and thrown away the design.

The run's whole record — four subagents' worth of investigation, design, implementation and proof — lives outside the target repo and outside git. Until 0.2.0 none of it reached GitHub before `ship`, which on the measured run never ran: 23 minutes of opus and sonnet output existed only as untracked files under $HOME and one unpushed commit. A gated pipeline that cannot survive losing the machine is a pipeline whose gates were the only thing it delivered.

prose.pattern: Never advance over drift you have not shown the user
prose.rationale: A run holds a model of the world it built at `start` and never checks again. On the measured run the change was pushed, merged, promoted and the issue closed while the run sat at a gate — and it then approved that stage, briefed the next one and dispatched a subagent against a branch whose pull request had already merged. Asking before advancing is the difference between a stale run and a wrong one.

prose.pattern: Never do a stage's work yourself
prose.rationale: Collapsing a stage into the orchestrator's own context destroys the isolation that makes each stage's artifact reviewable on its own, and produces an approval gate over work the approver has already been told the conclusion of.

prose.pattern: the red team is the gate, and it is a dispatched subagent — never you
prose.rationale: Auto mode removes the human from the gate, so the gate that replaces them must have the same independence: a reviewer that shares the orchestrator's context has already been told the conclusion it is supposed to attack. This extends the-orchestrator-does-no-stage-work to the review itself.

prose.pattern: Never weaken a review to clear a finding
prose.rationale: The eval and skillfactory rule, adopted verbatim, because an autonomous loop makes it more dangerous, not less: round 3 under a rounds cap is exactly when 'fix the reviewer' becomes cheaper than 'fix the work', and nobody is watching. The registrar refuses uncited findings; this line is what refuses the opposite move.

prose.pattern: Never auto-ship over an open blocking finding
prose.rationale: The rounds cap stops the loop; this stops the loop's failure from being laundered into a pull request. An exhausted stage surfaces its findings to the user and the run ends there — an auto run that ships anyway has turned the red team into decoration.

`--force` exists so a human who has re-read the drift can overrule it. An unattended run has nobody who re-read anything: blocking drift, like an exhausted stage, stops the run and surfaces — the flag is the one gate bypass in the CLI, and auto mode is exactly the caller that must never hold it.

deterministic.step: read the open issues and the repo's branch and pull request policy
fetch the chosen issue and its comments to disk and open the stage state machine
render each stage's dispatch prompt, model and subagent type from the approved artifacts
enforce the gate — record an artifact, record the approval, advance only then
register a completed red-team review — validate every citation, derive the verdict from the severities, bind it to the artifact's hash, record the round
expand an approved design's work items into stacked child lanes
report the state of an interrupted run so it resumes without guessing
list every run on this machine, so a run can be found without remembering its directory
push the branch and open the pull request under the repo's own policy
verify each lane's pull request merged, remove its worktree, delete its local branch, and write the run's terminal state

nondeterministic.step: what the issue actually asks for, and what its root cause is
nondeterministic.why: an issue is a person's description of a symptom; nothing on disk says which code causes it or whether the reporter asked for the right fix

nondeterministic.step: the design — the approach chosen, and the approaches rejected
nondeterministic.why: trade-offs between working designs are judgment; a file records the code that exists, never the one that should

nondeterministic.step: whether this issue is one change or several, and where the seams fall
nondeterministic.why: size signals suggest a split, they never locate it — only reading the design tells you which parts can land and be reviewed alone

nondeterministic.step: the implementation itself, written to match the surrounding code
nondeterministic.why: matching a codebase's idiom, naming and comment density is imitation, which no rule set encodes

nondeterministic.step: whether the tests actually prove the issue is fixed
nondeterministic.why: a green suite proves the tests passed, not that they tested the reported behaviour — only reading the issue against the assertions answers that

nondeterministic.step: whether an artifact is good enough to approve
nondeterministic.why: this is the user's call and the whole point of the gate; a skill that decides it has removed the thing it exists to provide — or, on an auto run, the red team's call, registered and hash-bound, with every round shown to the user

nondeterministic.step: what the stage missed — the adversarial hunt itself
nondeterministic.why: the registrar can check that a finding cites something real; only a reviewer reading the work can find the alternate root cause nobody ruled out, the file the design forgot, or the assertion that passes without the fix

_baseline_comment: Pinned against a real run of this skill against natejswenson/local-fitness#133 — its real open issue list, its real issue payload, and the investigation and design a real opus subagent produced from the briefs this skill rendered. Offline and $0 by construction: the frozen gh payloads are fed in through --repo-json/--issues-json/--issue-json, so CI cannot spend and cannot flake.

baseline.rationale: The state machine is re-run over the frozen inputs and byte-compared, so this fails when behaviour changes rather than when a fixture is edited. Catches the pick-table's columns or the run board drifting, and — the expensive one — a stage brief that silently stopped carrying the artifact it inherits, which is invisible at the call site and shows up only as a subagent redoing work already done. Since 0.2.0 it also pins the sticky issue comment, which is the ONLY artifact of a run that leaves the machine: a comment that lost the board, lost an approved artifact, or grew a local path is a run that cannot be recovered or a home directory published to a public issue, and nothing else in the repo would notice. A floor of 3 issue rows on the frozen board, an assertion that the Detail column still reports more than one value, and a 5 000-byte floor plus an empty-Took assertion on the comment stop a fixture refresh that collapsed every input to 'nothing to report' from passing this golden over nothing.

The known-bad side, without which the golden goes green the day the gate stops refusing anything. Drives a run whose design artifact is real and complete on disk and whose ONLY defect is that nobody approved it, then asserts brief, accept and ship all exit non-zero — plus that a skipped stage is still not a pass. Verified non-vacuous: stubbing blockers() to return [] turns eight tests red across this file and gate.test.mjs.

0.2.0 replaced the gate's flat prefix scan with a real dependency graph, which LOOSENS it — so it needs a two-sided pair, not a single assertion. One half proves a stacked lane still cannot be implemented before the lane it branches off (the loosening opened no hole); the other proves a lane CAN be implemented while the lane below it is still being tested (the concurrency is real rather than decorative). Either half alone passes over a graph that is wrong in the other direction, which is exactly how a parallelism feature ends up shipping as a comment. A third case asserts a hole two levels down is still named rather than hidden behind the step above it.

Checkpointing at every gate puts `gh` and `git push` on the path of `accept`, which every eval also calls. The stub IS the assertion: a `gh` on PATH that records being run, and an offline run that must never produce that file. Without it the baseline evals would quietly start reaching the network — spending money, flaking, and breaking the promise that `ci / issueflow` costs $0 — and would still go green. A second case pins that the flag lives on the RUN rather than the invocation, so a later bare `accept --run-dir` cannot dial out either.

Concurrent lanes are only safe because each works in its own checkout, and the test stage's revert-and-rerun proof is only safe for the same reason — before 0.2.0 it ran in the user's live tree. Drives a real temporary git repository: a lane's worktree is on its own branch and outside the repo, a second provisioning does not disturb work in progress, a commit made in the worktree is visible to the main checkout (the property `ship` depends on), and removing the worktree keeps the branch. The last case is the one that found a real bug: `git` walks upwards to find a repository, so a run pointed at a subdirectory created a branch in the ENCLOSING repo — the first offline eval run of this feature left a stray `feature/issue-133` branch in claude-skills itself.

Every shipped stage frozen with its full contract — model, agent, artifact, asks, requires, forbids. Catches a stage losing a field, and specifically a stage changing model, which changes what every run of it costs and how good it is while nothing else in the repo notices. The floor of 4 is the anti-vacuity rule: a state machine that lost a stage still renders as a complete-looking board, so a resolver matching fewer than four files must go red rather than report the remainder as clean.

Both fully-shipped runs `finish` was written to close still reported `ready to ship` forever, because nothing recorded that `ship` or `finish` had ever run (#219). Two-sided over a real temporary git repository with a stubbed `gh`: a lane whose pull request GitHub reports MERGED gets its worktree removed, its local branch deleted, and the landing recorded; a lane whose pull request is still OPEN, has none at all, or whose `gh` call fails is left completely untouched — the only path to `git branch -D` is a merge GitHub confirmed. A partially-landed split run finishes the merged lane, leaves the open one intact, and completes when `finish` runs again without redoing the first lane's work. `--close-issue` closes an open issue and reports an already-closed one as already closed rather than claiming an action it did not take, and an offline run refuses outright rather than finishing on an assumption.

`runs` used to discard a `RunError` that `loadRun` already writes to be actionable, rendering a schema-1 run as a bare `(unreadable run)` with no reason and no remedy — the reader could not even tell which issue the directory belonged to (#223). Drives a run root holding one schema-1 run alongside one valid schema-2 run: the unreadable row keeps its directory name in `Title` and names the schema mismatch and the remedy `loadRun` already wrote, in the same table the readable row still renders its repo/issue id, title and approved count — the bound `catch` must not have swallowed the readable rows too. A fourth assertion pins that the reason's full text, path included, lands below the table and never inside a padded cell, extending the existing rule that a padded cell holding an absolute path encodes the host's tmpdir.

`Took` used to answer only after a human typed `accept`: `at.delivered` is written in exactly one place, so `briefed` / `—` was the entire liveness signal for a stage that had, in fact, been running for minutes or had already finished and was waiting for review (#223). Two-sided: a step that is briefed with no artifact on disk shows a live elapsed `Took` suffixed `+` (a lower bound, never a finished duration); the same step once an artifact lands — still unaccepted — shows a `delivered` display state and a real duration with no `+`. A third case proves the clock does not start early on a step that was never dispatched. Two purity guards close the loop: `observe(dir, run)` never writes `run.json` and never mutates the run object handed to it, and the `delivered` value it predicts equals what `accept()` later persists for the same artifact; and `board(run)` called with no `now` renders no `+` anywhere and matches the pre-#223 shape exactly, which is what keeps the live clock from leaking into a frozen golden or the public checkpoint comment.

The registrar is the anti-hallucination gate for the red team, and it needs both sides: a review with a cited note registers hash-bound, while a citation naming a file that does not exist, a heading the artifact lacks, or a line past EOF refuses the WHOLE review and writes no verdict — a finding that cites nothing is an opinion. Also refuses a finding line off the declared grammar (a finding that fails to parse silently stops existing), a declared pass over a high finding (the severities decide, not the reviewer's summary of itself), and zero findings above an empty Not examined section — 'clean' without naming what nobody looked at is indistinguishable from 'unreviewed', the eval skill's coverage rule as code.

The mirror of the unapproved-stage trap, for the gate that replaces the human. accept --auto must refuse: a run not started --auto (which gate holds a run is decided once, at start), no registered review, a blocked round, an artifact edited after its review (the verdict binds to the sha of the bytes it read), and — driven against a real git repository — a commit landed after a code review (the branch moved under the verdict). The good side approves and records autoApproved, and a plain human accept still works on an auto run. Without the bad side, weakening any one binding check leaves auto mode approving work its red team never saw.

Three blocked rounds is where the loop stops converging and must stop running. Drives the real CLI over a run with three registered blocked rounds: a fourth brief of the stage and a fourth review brief both exit non-zero, auto-accept still refuses, and ship still refuses the run — exhaustion surfaces to the user, it never rounds up to shipped. Two-sided: below the cap the loop continues, and the re-brief carries the blocked round's findings verbatim, which is the feedback seam a refused stage used to lack.

Every shipped reviewer frozen with its full contract, same discipline as the stage corpus: one reviewer per stage, in stage order, each on opus — the red team is the judgment an auto run pays for, and a reviewer quietly moved to a cheaper model is a gate that rubber-stamps while every board still looks complete. The floor of 4 stops a resolver that matches nothing from reporting an unguarded pipeline as fully reviewed.

baseline.update_command: field-project this repo's own current run.json for issue-212/215/219 under evals/inputs/timings/ — schema/repo/issue/stages/lanes[].stages and their `at` timestamps only, no artifact prose and no prompt text (see the dispatch-expectation implement notes for the exact shape); there is no scripted regenerator because these are frozen real runs, not a re-derivable fixture
baseline.rationale: `brief`'s expectation line (`design on this repo: 3 past runs, 3m45s–6m45s (median 5m12s)`) reads real prior-run durations off the run's sibling directories, and the anti-vacuity floor is the whole point: a `readTimings` that matched nothing would silently degrade to `no past timings on this repo` and pass every other liveness assertion, which is exactly how this feature goes decorative. The floor of 3 is this repo's own #212/#215/#219 runs, and a companion test asserts the scan over them finds at least 10 individual stage samples, not just 3 files — a resolver that opened the directories but extracted nothing would still clear a file-count floor alone.
